title: Generated levels
author: Bright_Owl_9275
selftext: I have to ask, like others I am vibe coding my first game. I am pretty familiar with AI as I use it on my day-to-day as a software engineer, but as I vibe code my first 2D mobile game, I have come across an issue and experience it frequently. In my escape room game each room is a prefab. The room prefabs are essentially empty, and I have a system in place that will auto place other smaller prefabs into the room. Things like chairs and desks and cabinets. I’m having to constantly go back-and-forth with the AI to tell it how these items should be placed, but it seems like a lot of effort and tokens wasted. As someone with no experience I just have to ask how are people dealing with this? I’m taking a very vibe coated approach, but is there some sort of formula that I should’ve followed from the start to not have to deal with this? Do I have to go in and manually decorate the rooms and save the prefabs or can I be totally hands off? I approached this project as an overnight MVP, generating a full level with a handful of items, but now looking back, I wonder if this approach was even viable. Or should I have been working piece by piece, designing each room before putting it all together

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
Can’t you just… put things where you want? Drag them to the right place? This doesn’t sound like an effective use of AI.

Just manually place them, it should be fast.

comments.author: HarlequinStar
comments.body:
The traditional approach for these kinds of things is to just have a number of 'points'/coordinates and have the system randomly choose which points it uses and place things in those points. Some more advanced ones will even have tags or settings for the points that can let you restrict what kind of things the system can put at them.

For example, in Spelunky, many of the rooms have 'optional' platforms and pickup locations that the randomiser will turn on or off to make the rooms feel different in addition to the random construction from the prefabs it does.

Not sure how you'd apply that to an AI framework though :o

replies.author: Bright_Owl_9275
replies.body: That’s good. That’s exactly the pattern I was heading towards. Though the point placement is what I think I might have to do manually. I have tried saying things like “center of the room”, or “in the corners”. It’s just a waste. I’m thinking if I add special tags to all of my prefabs, I can then just add  invisible objects in the prefabs and choose from a list what sort of tags are allowed there. And based on the rooms orientation control which sprite to use. I have 4 angles per sprite for each compass direction

replies.author: HarlequinStar
replies.body: Sounds like it'd work! I hope it leads to the results you're after :D

replies.author: Jolva
replies.body: Do you know how to move things around yourself? If you're using Unity, you can use the game view or scene view, then click objects to move them around on their axis. Way easier to fine tune that way.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: If your engine doesn't already allow manual placement based on what you're building, have your AI build a level editor for you, then build the levels yourself.

comments.author: Fulgren09
comments.body:
Since you are using AI, get your agent to write a guide for placing objects in a room when it auto gens it. Separate the 'view' from the 'floor plan' layer. Get it to think about the surface area budget of where objects will be placed.

Have it create an evaluation loop before it renders the room. The idea is that this is a random dice roll where you can help rig the result.
